title: Tier II Checkpoint I — An Integrated Lesson

pts: Set an aim that names more than grammar — a sociolinguistic or discourse goal alongside the linguistic one.
Build in a moment for strategic competence practice, such as a deliberately withheld key word.
This keeps the lesson's aim aligned with the full model, not just its grammatical quarter.

items: Write the linguistic aim.
Add a sociolinguistic aim (appropriacy for the audience).
Add a discourse aim (organizing the recommendation).
Add a strategic aim (coping when a word is missing).
Check that each aim is visible in at least one stage of the lesson.
Share aims with learners in simplified form on the board.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Linguistic: use comparatives and ‘should/would’ to compare and recommend.
Sociolinguistic: make a polite recommendation to the headteacher.
Discourse: organize a spoken recommendation in three moves.
Strategic: explain a place feature when a key word is unknown.
Today we will choose the best place for our class trip and persuade the headteacher.

pts: Open with a brief pre-task, move into the task itself with monitoring only, then into planning and report stages.
Save explicit language work for the post-task language-focus stage, based on what the task actually surfaced.
This is the lesson's core structural backbone, not an occasional lesson format among many.

items: Pre-task (10 minutes): extract from the reader; introduce the topic and the task.
Task (15 minutes): groups share information and choose a destination; the teacher monitors only.
Planning (15 minutes): groups prepare a one-minute recommendation.
Report (20 minutes): selected groups present; the class votes.
Language focus (15 minutes): work on language that the task surfaced.
Close (5 minutes): feedback and group processing.
Across two single periods, end the first after planning, so the report opens the next lesson.
Support: display the stages and times on the board for learners.
Challenge: groups plan their own time within the planning stage.

lines: Read → Share → Choose → Plan → Present → Language → Reflect.

blocks.x: During the task, the teacher does not correct. Notes go into a notebook for the language focus. This is Unit 28’s task cycle used as the backbone of the lesson, not an occasional variation.

pts: Decide explicitly whether this lesson's task prioritises fluency, accuracy or complexity, and design accordingly.
Communicate that priority to learners so their performance is judged against the intended dimension.
Plan a different priority for the next lesson in the sequence, echoing Unit 29's course-level sequencing advice.

items: Decide the task’s main priority: here, fluency during the task and a degree of complexity in the report.
Tell learners what that means: keep talking; don’t stop for small mistakes.
Build in planning time to support complexity in the report (Skehan 1998).
Note that accuracy will be the priority in the next lesson, where groups write the recommendation.
Give learners a simple self-rating: Did I keep talking? Did I use a longer sentence?
Support: fluency first; complexity optional.
Challenge: use at least one sentence with because or although.

lines: T: Today, I want you to speak as much as you can. Mistakes are OK. Next week, when we write the letter, we will make it perfect.
Lesson 1: fluency (discussion). Lesson 2: complexity (planned report). Lesson 3: accuracy (written letter).

blocks.x: Learners judge themselves against the stated priority, not against a vague idea of ‘good English’ (Unit 29).

body: Purpose: to show a declared priority. Content: a dial with three sectors, fluency, accuracy and complexity, and a needle pointing at fluency; a small calendar shows the needle moving in later lessons. Style: simple. Board version: a semicircle with an arrow.

items: None needed; the priority is written on the board.

pts: Ensure the task has a real information or opinion gap that requires genuine negotiation of meaning to resolve.
Model a clarification request or confirmation check explicitly before the task begins.
Note recurring negotiation breakdowns during monitoring for the language-focus stage.

items: Each group member gets a card with information about one factor: distance, cost, what to see, facilities.
Each card covers all three places (Hampi, Mysuru, Jog Falls) for one factor.
Before the task, model a clarification request and a confirmation check.
Learners share information orally without showing cards.
The group chooses one place and gives two reasons.
Add an opinion gap: each learner has a personal preference card (You love history).
Support: the facilities card has fewer details and pictures.
Challenge: the cost card includes figures that must be calculated.

lines: T: If you don’t understand, what can you say?
Ss: Sorry, can you say that again?
T: And to check?
Ss: So you mean…?
S1: For Jog Falls, the… the money at the gate is less.
S2: You mean the ticket?
S1: Yes, the ticket price.

blocks.x: This is negotiation of meaning in action (Long 1996; Unit 30). The teacher notes breakdowns, such as learners saying What? and nothing more, for the language focus.

body: Purpose: to show an information gap. Content: four learners on a bench each holding a different card (a road, a rupee symbol, a monument, a toilet and food icon), with speech bubbles showing questions and answers. Style: friendly. Board version: four card shapes with symbols.

pts: Tie the lesson's topic to what's currently being read or listened to extensively, reinforcing vocabulary incidentally.
Use a short extract from a graded reader or extensive-listening source as the pre-task's schema activation.
This keeps extensive input and classroom teaching mutually reinforcing rather than running as separate tracks.

v: A short extract from the class graded reader or a two-minute audio

items: Read aloud, or play, a short extract describing a journey.
Learners listen for two things: Where did they go? How did they feel?
Pairs recall useful words (crowded, beautiful, tiring).
Ask: Where would you like to go on a class trip?
Introduce the task.
Use a learner-recommended podcast episode about travel from the class listening chart (Unit 32).
Support: key words on the board before listening.
Challenge: learners retell the extract in three sentences.

lines: The bus left before sunrise. By the time we reached Hampi, the rocks were glowing orange. Ammu said it looked like another planet. We were tired, but nobody wanted to go back.

blocks.x: Vocabulary met here recurs in the task and in the reader, so incidental learning is reinforced (Day and Bamford 1998). Extensive input and classroom teaching support each other rather than running as separate tracks.

body: Purpose: to show the link between extensive input and the lesson. Content: a graded reader open on a desk, with words floating from it (crowded, beautiful, tiring) into a group discussion bubble above a bench. Style: warm. Board version: a book with arrows to a speech bubble.

points.h: Frame the Output as a Genre
pts: Give the task's report stage a real genre target — a short pitch, a recommendation, a complaint — not just 'talk about it.'
Briefly analyse the genre's typical structure before learners produce their own version.
This raises the transferability of the lesson's output beyond this one classroom task.

items: Show a model one-minute recommendation (see model language).
Learners identify three moves: recommendation, reasons, polite request.
Point out polite language for addressing the headteacher.
Groups plan their recommendation following the moves.
Each member rehearses one move.
Change the genre: a written notice or a short letter.
Support: sentence starters for each move.
Challenge: add a move that answers an objection (Some people may say it is too far, but…).

lines: [Recommendation] Good morning, madam. Our group recommends Mysuru for the class trip.
[Reasons] First, it is only three hours away. Second, the palace and the zoo are both educational. Finally, it is cheaper than Hampi.
[Request] We hope you will consider our suggestion. Thank you.

blocks.x: A genre target makes the report stage more than ‘talk about it’ (Unit 33) and gives learners a structure they can use outside class.

body: Purpose: to show a spoken genre structure. Content: a learner at the front holding three cue cards, each coloured and labelled with a move, facing a friendly headteacher. Style: cheerful. Board version: three stacked boxes.

pts: Assign clear roles and build genuine interdependence into the task's information distribution.
Close with brief group processing — how did the group work together, not just what did they produce.
This ensures the lesson's group work is cooperative learning in the full sense, not just seating arrangement.

v: Throughout the task and planning; 3 minutes at the end

items: Assign roles in each group of four: reporter, timekeeper, language monitor, questioner.
Explain each role briefly.
Remind the class of this week’s social skill: inviting a quiet member.
After the report, groups answer two processing questions.
Rotate roles next lesson.
Groups of five for very large classes, adding a note-taker role.
Support: a new learner takes the timekeeper role with a simple card.
Challenge: the questioner prepares one difficult question for another group.

lines: Reporter: presents the recommendation. Timekeeper: keeps to time. Language monitor: reminds the group to use English for key decisions. Questioner: makes sure everyone speaks.
What helped our group work well? What will we do differently next time?

blocks.x: Interdependence comes from the information cards; accountability comes from roles and the rehearsal of one move each. That makes this cooperative learning in the full sense of Unit 34, not simply a seating arrangement.

body: Purpose: to show structured roles. Content: four learners on a fixed bench, each wearing a small badge with a role icon (microphone, clock, speech bubble with ‘EN’, question mark). Style: friendly, realistic. Board version: four stick figures with symbols.

items: Share two or three good examples noticed during the task, including strategic ones.
Share one negotiation problem and practise a better phrase.

After the lesson, log recurring patterns.
Use the log to set the aims for the next lesson.
Learners write one ‘I learned’ sentence as an exit slip.

T: Some groups forgot to ask the headteacher politely at the end. What can we say?

Good: paraphrase strategies. Problem: ‘What?’ as the only clarification. Next lesson: accuracy focus on the written letter; revisit clarification phrases.

dek: Unit 35 of 100: closing the opening stretch of Tier II by walking one fully integrated-skills lesson, showing where Units 26 through 34 meet in a single class.

aims.x: This unit closes the opening stretch of Part II. Instead of introducing new theory, it walks through one integrated-skills lesson and shows where the ideas of Units 26–34 meet in a single class. The lesson is designed for a real Indian secondary classroom: about fifty learners, fixed benches, a blackboard and perhaps one phone for audio. Each point below is one layer of the same lesson.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: write lesson aims that cover more than grammar;
structure a lesson around the task cycle;
decide and announce the lesson’s fluency, accuracy or complexity priority;
build an information gap that requires negotiation of meaning;
link a lesson to learners’ extensive reading and listening;
give the task’s report stage a genre target;
organize groups cooperatively, with roles and processing;
close a lesson with feedback and a log that shapes the next one.

why: Why this matters. Nine posters of theory and technique only prove their worth combined. This checkpoint is the proof of concept before Tier II moves to project and course scale.

background.x: Units 26–34 each examined one part of teaching for integrated skills: the overall model (Unit 26), communicative competence (Unit 27), the task cycle (Unit 28), fluency, accuracy and complexity (Unit 29), negotiation of meaning (Unit 30), extensive reading and listening (Units 31–32), genre (Unit 33) and cooperative learning (Unit 34). Separately, each is useful. Their real value appears when they work together, and when a teacher can see how one decision affects another. A genre target, for example, changes what counts as a successful task; cooperative roles change who speaks during negotiation.

The lesson in this unit is built on Jane Willis’s (1996) task framework: pre-task, task cycle (task, planning, report) and language focus. Its aims draw on the model of communicative competence developed by Canale and Swain (1980) and extended by Celce-Murcia, Dörnyei and Thurrell (1995). Its choice of priority follows Skehan’s (1998) argument that learners’ attention is limited, so that task design and conditions push performance towards fluency, accuracy or complexity. Its information gap follows Long’s (1996) interaction hypothesis. Its link to reading follows Day and Bamford (1998), its genre work Swales (1990), and its group structure Johnson and Johnson (2009).

The lesson is set in Class 9 of a government high school in Karnataka, with learners at roughly A2+/B1. The class is reading a graded reader about a journey, and the school is planning an educational trip. The task is to recommend a destination to the headteacher. This is an authentic purpose: schools do plan trips, and learners do have views. It reflects the NCF 2023 emphasis on meaningful, real-life language use (NCERT 2023) and allows home languages in planning, as NEP 2020 encourages (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). The lesson fits two 40-minute periods, or one double period.

items: Recommendation performance. Rate each group’s spoken recommendation on moves, clarity and politeness.
Negotiation checklist. During monitoring, tick clarification requests and confirmation checks used.
Exit slips. One sentence from each learner on what they learned.
Lesson audit. Teachers evaluate their lesson against the eight points and set one improvement.

terms.def: The knowledge and ability needed to use language appropriately in real situations, including grammar, social appropriacy, discourse and strategy, not only grammatical correctness (Hymes 1972).
Roles assigned to group members, such as writer, speaker and checker, that share out participation and responsibility during a task.
The genre that a task’s outcome should take, such as a one-minute spoken recommendation. Setting it changes what counts as a successful task and focuses the report and language-focus stages.
An activity in which learners hold different information and must communicate to complete a task, such as finding differences between two pictures or completing a timetable.
A lesson in which several skills work together towards one outcome, often built on a task cycle with a genre target and cooperative roles.
A stage in a lesson, especially at the end of a task cycle, where learners examine and practise language features that arose during the task (Willis 1996).
A brief record kept by the teacher of what happened in a lesson, including good examples and problems noticed while monitoring, used to plan feedback and later lessons.
The interactional work, such as clarification requests and comprehension checks, that speakers do to resolve breakdowns in understanding; it is claimed to help acquisition (Long 1996).
In task-based teaching, the stage before the main task that introduces the topic, activates vocabulary and may include planning or modelling.
The central phase of a task-based lesson, in which learners do the task, plan a report and present it to the class (Willis 1996). It is preceded by a pre-task and followed by a language focus.
